analysis.one_liner: Requires strict mercury pollution controls on coal- and oil-fired power plants within a year.
analysis.headline: The bill to mandate strict mercury controls on power plants was referred to a House subcommittee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to require the EPA to set the toughest available pollution-control standards for mercury emissions from electric utility steam generating units — mostly coal-fired power plants — taking effect one year after enactment. Mercury from power plants settles into waterways, builds up in fish, and is a known neurotoxin that is especially harmful to pregnant women and young children. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it sat until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people — especially communities near coal plants, anglers and their families, pregnant women, and children — gain reduced mercury exposure, which lowers risks of neurological and developmental harm. Waterways and fish ecosystems also benefit as mercury deposition declines.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to set standards for mercury emissions from electric utility steam generating units under the MACT (maximum achievable control technology) framework for hazardous air pollutants, effective one year after enactment [S2][S3].

The MACT framework is the strictest of the Clean Air Act's hazardous-pollution approaches, requiring plants to match the emission controls already achieved by the best-performing plants rather than a trading scheme [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and oil-fired power plants — and their customers through electricity rates — would bear the cost of installing and operating mercury emission controls within the one-year deadline.

drawbacks.text: The one-year effective deadline in the bill is aggressive for retrofits of hundreds of generating units; utilities and ratepayers could face steep capital costs passed through electricity bills, and some older plants might retire sooner than grid operators planned [S3].

Critics of MACT-style regulation argued the cost per ton of mercury removed was high compared with alternatives, such as emissions trading, making this a more expensive route to the same health benefit (general policy debate around utility mercury rules of the era).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit — less mercury in fish, water, and children — is real and borne by the public broadly, while the cost falls mainly on plant operators and ratepayers, and it is concentrated in the utility sector. The very short deadline could have made compliance more expensive than a phased approach, but the bill's substance is a public-health gain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality on February 16, 2007, and never advanced to a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Eddie Bernice Johnson introduced the Mercury Emissions Reduction Act on February 15, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].

The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, which is where the bill's record ends; no further action appears through the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].
The bill had 5 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal- and oil-fired electric utilities avoided a mandate to install maximum achievable control technology for mercury on a one-year timeline, saving retrofit costs, and their customers avoided any associated rate increase. People exposed to mercury from power-plant emissions got no new protections from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Eddie Bernice Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought strict mercury emission standards for power plants

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality and never scheduled it for markup or floor action during the two-year Congress

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing or markup for the remainder of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support on record was Democratic — a Democratic sponsor with 5 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans — and the bill died without any vote, so no party-split roll call exists [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have required these plants to install maximum achievable control technology for mercury within a year, a major capital cost. The utility industry's interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the public's interest in lower mercury exposure; the bill died, so the industry kept the status quo.
Stricter mercury controls on coal plants would have reduced coal burn or accelerated retirements of some units, cutting coal demand. The bill's failure left coal demand unchanged.

Vendors of activated-carbon injection and other mercury control systems would have gained a large retrofit market; with no mandate, that market grew only later under different rules. Their interest in the bill was aligned with the public's interest in cleaner air.
